The U-3 is the number they're quoting, and politicians love it because it has the broadest possible definition of "employed": If you worked at least 1 hour in the previous week, for gainful employment, then you're employed. The number you want to look at is the U-6 (that's the one you'll hear referred to as the "real" unemployment rate), which has been, and still is, over 10% (10.3% to be exact) since the recession.

The other key factor to remember, especially when you hear people talking about "X number of jobs were added last month", is that, by the most conservative estimate, we need roughly 85,000 jobs each month just to "break even" (i.e. keep up with the population growth), so take those numbers with a grain of salt.

It's strange that "all persons marginally attached to the labor force" is mentioned twice. With U-3 you've got unemployed divided by the labor force, but with U-4,5,6 what counts as unemployed and employed is increasing.

That's mostly because the U-3 has such a broad definition of "employed" that, in and of itself, it doesn't really tell us anything useful; it tells us how many people are unemployed, but it doesn't give us any context, and without context that number is meaningless.
